title: Stopping the band and silent breaks
summary: Allen asks about the silent pause before the band resumes; Jones calls it a tag.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You know, that Fulham business reminds me. When I used to go here, Joe Avery and Wilbert Tillman up at Towers, Big Garden up by Adam and Buck, I don't know if he ever said it. But they'd play a number, and they'd come to the end, and they'd stop. Now, I don't know how many, whether they'd just stop for a bar or two. And then all of a sudden, they'd start up again, and it was a way of Fulham,
Not when they'd stop like that, with the drummers.
Did you ever hear that, Bill? I've heard some breaks, though. I don't know whether it's intentional. What do you say that one?
No, Bache does it. Bache does that on Shake It and Break It. That record, I don't know if you remember it. But the band will stop.
Oh, you mean that's a break.

No, no. Nobody's. You mean it's a break? No, not a break. But they come to the end of the chorus, and then stop, and everybody thinks the tune is over, and then they start up again after a certain number of beats. I forget.
Was that a taxi dance for you? Somebody was working on it?
No, it wasn't a taxi dance.

Well, what he's talking about, that's just trying to... The thing I was saying about this guy... It's like Putin. Like a tag. When they come to that, and everybody stop, man. And all of a sudden, the drum pick up. Then they start right on back with that number again. I have seen them do that a lot of times, occasionally.
